questions.q: What does the "lost in the middle" effect describe?
options: Models cannot process context windows larger than 10,000 tokens
Models always ignore the system prompt
Tool schemas are never usable once history grows
Content placed near the start or end of a long context is recalled more reliably than content buried in the middle, even when everything fits in budget
questions.explain: The lesson describes a documented effect: recall is strongest near the start and end of a context window and weakest in the middle, independent of whether content fits within the token budget.

questions.q: According to the ordering recipe, where should lower-priority background material go?
options: At the very start of the context window
In the middle of the context window, since it can tolerate weaker recall
It should never be included at all
Immediately after the user's question
questions.explain: The recipe places lower-priority content in the middle deliberately, since that's the weakest position for recall — reserving it for content that matters least.

questions.q: Where does the recipe say the single most relevant retrieved chunk should be placed?
options: Wherever the retrieval step happened to rank it in its own output
At the very start of the context window, before the system prompt
Right before the user's question, near the end of the window
In the middle, alongside background documents
questions.explain: The recipe places the best-matching chunk right before the user's question, in the strong end-of-window position, not wherever a retrieval step ranked it internally.

questions.q: Why does the lesson treat ranking and placement as two separate decisions?
options: Because a chunk can be correctly ranked as most relevant by a retrieval step, yet still end up assembled into the weak middle position of the final context
Because ranking and placement are always identical in practice
Because placement only applies to tool schemas, not retrieved content
Because ranking is done by the user, not the system
questions.explain: A relevance-ranking step and the final assembly order are different steps; correctly ranking content first doesn't guarantee it lands in a strong position unless placement is handled deliberately.

questions.q: A response misses a fact that was genuinely present in the context and within the token budget. What does this lesson say is worth checking?
options: Whether the model's output format was JSON or plain text
Whether the user asked the question twice
Whether the system prompt was written in the wrong language
Whether the fact was placed in a weak position (like the middle) rather than whether it was cut for budget reasons
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes a budget problem (content was compressed or cut) from a position problem (content was present in full but sat in the weakest recall position), each requiring a different fix.
